newsitem.title: TAIWAN: POLL-Taiwan July CPI seen rising 3.40 pct.
newsitem.headline: POLL-Taiwan July CPI seen rising 3.40 pct.

text.p: A Reuters Poll of Taiwan economists on Monday projected a 3.40 percent in year-on-year consumer price index growth for July.
The official figures were scheduled to be issued at 0300 GMT on August 5 by the cabinet's Directorate General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics.
June's CPI growth was 1.84 percent year-on-year.
The following table gives institutions' forecasts for year-on-year growth in July of Taiwan's consumer prices, in percent:
Institution CPI growth
Core Pacific Securities 2.81
Grand Cathay Securities 3.90
National Securities 4.0
HSBC James Capel Taiwan 2.90
Nomura Securities 3.40
Average 3.40
Economists said they expected July's consumer prices to rise significantly compared with previous months partly due to heavy torrential rains that hit the island severely in June and July.
The flood seriously damaged crops, driving up food -- particularly vegetable, -- prices, economists said.
The directorate has said that vegetable prices would remain high in July.
In the first six months, Taiwan's CPI grew 1.37 percent year-on-year, still falling well below the directorate's estimate of 2.01 pecent for whole 1997 CPI growth.
A low basis in July 1996 also contribued to the expected high annual growth.
"July 1996's CPI was extremely low at 1.44 percent -- the lowest level in that year," HSBC James Capel economist Stephen Wang said. "We are comparing with a very low basis."
"Food prices will be relatively high because of the floods, while prices in other sectors will remain stable," Wang said.
The poor weather already drove June vegetable prices up an annual 18.98 percent and 35.51 percent from May.
Vegetable prices account for about three percent of the total CPI weighting.
In the broader category, food prices rose 4.78 percent month-on-month in June.
Most economists said they expected the CPI to stabilise in August or September.
"July's high CPI will likely be an individual case, affected by seasonal factors. It does not mean we will see high CPI growth in the following months," said National Securities economist Eric Lin.
"In fact, CPI will probably return to low growth in August and September," Lin said.
The cabinet's Council for Economic Planning and Development has set a 1997 CPI growth target of 3.0 percent.
In March, the central bank revised its forecast for 1997 CPI growth to around 3.0 percent from 3.31 percent.
-- Taipei Newsroom (2-5080815)
